claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 treated above 1200 °C is a homogeneous, disordered, single-phase BCC alloy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the BCC phase of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at high temperature.
The high-temperature BCC phase becomes thermodynamically unstable during cooling.
Al exerts a strong chemical influence that initiates local ordering in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Al-induced local ordering lowers the alloy's free energy.
Phase stability is governed by competition between high-temperature entropy stabilization and a composition-dependent chemical-ordering tendency.
Sufficient atomic mobility during cooling enables the proposed chemical ordering.
Cooling rate can control phase selection in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow cooling permits local atomic rearrangement and subtle chemical segregation, particularly around Al.
Local rearrangement and Al-centered segregation facilitate nucleation of an ordered phase.
Slow cooling may transform the BCC alloy into an FCC or intermetallic-like ordered phase.
Rapid quenching kinetically suppresses ordering.
Rapid quenching retains metastable BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow cooling produces a significant ordered-phase fraction relative to the high-temperature BCC baseline.
Ordering after slow cooling will produce detectable diffraction and local chemical-environment differences.
The operative ordering window is approximately 1200 °C to 600 °C.
Above the proposed temperature window, kinetic barriers are too high for marked transformation.
Below the proposed temperature window, diffusion is too sluggish for marked transformation.
The identity and volume fraction of the ordered product may depend on slight compositional deviations and processing details.
A lack of significant phase or ordering differences between quenched and slowly cooled samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism associates greater atomic mobility with thermally enabled ordering, whereas the boundary states that temperatures above the proposed window impose excessively high kinetic barriers. This reverses the usual temperature dependence of mobility and conflicts with the stated mobility-based explanation; suppression at high temperature would need to be attributed to thermodynamic disordering rather than high kinetic barriers.
